lec05kp26-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp26-u01-p8-title.text: What to remember: simplicity bias times a rare class, fixed by data or costs

lec05kp26-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp26-u01-p8-bridge.text: Changing the costs, like changing the data, raises TP and FP together and lowers precision. What should be remembered?

lec05kp26-u01-p8-nf-lec05-kp26-remember-.name: fig:lec05-kp26-remember|The harm of imbalance does not come from the numbers being different but from the interaction of the preference for simplicity with the rare class. Two remedies: change the data (resampling: over-, under- and focused undersampling) or change the costs (SVM class weights, AdaBoost initial weights). Common myth: high accuracy is enough; all-majority also has 98.0%, so look at recall and precision. Class imbalance matters a lot in practice, and designers must be aware of it and of the remedies (source).

lec05kp26-u01-p10-q1.name: u01-p10-q1
lec05kp26-u01-p10-q1.text: **Exercise 1**: 1000 negatives and 10 positives (the rare class). A: everything judged negative; B: catches 6 of the 10 positives and raises 40 false alarms among the negatives. What are the accuracy and the recall of A and of B?

lec05kp26-u01-p10-q2.name: u01-p10-q2
lec05kp26-u01-p10-q2.text: **Exercise 2**: what is the balanced accuracy of A and of B? (Hint: balanced accuracy $=(\text{recall}+\text{specificity})/2$, specificity $=\text{TN}/1000$.)

lec05kp26-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp26-u01-p11-title.text: Extension: A has accuracy 0.990 yet catches no rare point, and B has balanced accuracy 0.78

lec05kp26-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp26-u01-p11-bridge.text: Two exercises on accuracy, recall and balanced accuracy. Worked step by step, what are the answers?

lec05kp26-u01-p11-nf-lec05-kp26-solution.name: fig:lec05-kp26-solution|1000 negatives and 10 positives. A (all negative): TP 0, FN 10, FP 0, TN 1000, accuracy 1000/1010=0.990, recall 0, balanced accuracy (0+1)/2=0.5. B (6 caught, 40 false alarms): TP 6, FN 4, FP 40, TN 960, accuracy 966/1010=0.956, recall 6/10=0.6, specificity 960/1000=0.96, balanced accuracy (0.6+0.96)/2=0.78; B's precision is only 6/46=0.13, which is the trade-off.

steps.label: The class imbalance problem
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp26 with view-from-text-v2: the pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic, with the terms defined inside the same figure. 8 main pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). All experiments (means of 20 runs, training seeds 0 to 19, test seed 998, and 997 for the difficulty experiment) were designed for this lecture and generated by code; rerunning them reproduces the lecture's numbers cell by cell. The source provides the reasoning about the preference for simplicity, Japkowicz's conclusion on difficulty and data size, focused resampling, the open question of the target distribution and the 'how to remember' summary. Average counts are means of 20 integer counts, hence the decimals. English version.

steps.label: The setup
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP26, following KP25: AdaBoost degrades when labels are noisy. This unit asks: when one class has only 20 samples, is even high accuracy trustworthy? First, where all the numbers come from. The experiments were designed for this lecture and generated by code. Class imbalance means one class has very many samples and another very few, as in text classification, rare diseases and oil-slick detection. Data: the majority class is drawn from a standard normal centred at (0,0), the rare class from a standard normal centred at (2,0), with independent coordinates and standard deviation 1. Training uses 1000 plus 20 points; the test is one fixed set of 5000 plus 100 points with random seed 998, so the rare points are only 2%. The model is an RBF-kernel SVM with C equal to 1; the training set is drawn with seeds 0 to 19, 20 times, and averaged. The figure shows one training set: blue are majority points, orange squares are rare points; the two clouds overlap clearly, so they cannot be separated completely. The next page asks how to judge a classifier.

steps.label: From counts to metrics
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the rare points are only 2% of the test and the two clouds overlap clearly. This page asks how to judge a classifier and whether accuracy can see the rare class. On the left are the SVM's four counts, a mean of 20 runs: TP, the rare points caught, is 5.85; FN, the rare points missed, is 94.15; FP, the false alarms, is 2; TN, the majority points judged right, is 4998. Three metrics on the right: recall is the share of rare points caught, TP over TP plus FN; precision is the share of called-rare points that are truly rare, TP over TP plus FP; accuracy is the share of all points right, TP plus TN over 5100. Example 1, all-majority: TP 0 and FP 0, so recall is 0 and accuracy is 5000 over 5100, which is 98.0%. Example 2, the SVM: recall 5.85 over 100 is 5.9%; precision 5.85 over 5.85 plus 2 is 74.5%; accuracy 5.85 plus 4998 over 5100 is 98.1%. Precision is always computed from the mean counts. Accuracy hardly moves from 98.0% to 98.1% while recall goes from 0 to 5.9%: accuracy cannot see the rare class. The next page asks why a classifier ignores the rare class.

steps.label: The preference for simplicity
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that accuracy hardly moves from 98.0% to 98.1% while recall goes from 0 to 5.9%. This page asks why a classifier ignores the rare class. The source's reasoning: to generalise we keep demanding simple classifiers, through regularisation and pruning; a simple hypothesis does not bother with rare cases, and ignoring 20 points hardly changes the overall cost. The left chart is the SVM, where a larger C regularises less: for C equal to 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100 the recall is 0%, 0%, 5.9%, 13.5%, 16.9% and the accuracy in the grey boxes below is 98.0%, 98.0%, 98.1%, 98.2%, 98.2%. The right chart is the decision tree, CART with at least k points per leaf, where a larger k is simpler: for k equal to 50, 20, 5, 1 the recall is 0%, 9.5%, 21.0%, 23.3% and the accuracy 98.0%, 98.0%, 97.9%, 97.1%. The simpler it is, the fewer TP, down to all-majority, while accuracy stays near 98%. These are means of 20 runs with the fixed test of 5000 plus 100, seed 998. The next page asks whether imbalance is always bad.

steps.label: Difficulty and data size
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the simpler a classifier the less it cares about the rare points while accuracy stays near 98%. This page asks whether class imbalance is always bad. The source's conclusion comes from Japkowicz: a large imbalance is not necessarily harmful and must be read together with the task difficulty and the number of training points. Simple tasks or lots of data may be fine; hard tasks, with overlapping classes, or too few points can be fatal even at a small imbalance. The experiment was designed for this lecture: the same RBF SVM with C equal to 1 and gamma equal to 0.5; the training sets are majority to rare 100:100, 1000:100, 1000:10, 10000:100 and 10000:10; the test is fixed at 2000 plus 2000 with seed 997; the two class centres are 4 apart for the easy task and 1.5 apart for the hard one. The heat map shows the recall of the rare class: easy 97.5%, 91.6%, 66.8%, 78.1%, 43.2%; hard 78.6%, 14.9%, 0.0%, 0.0%, 0.0%. With only 10 rare points even the easy task is poor; on the hard task 1000 against 100 already presses the recall to 14.9%. Note that these are 10 cells, not a monotone trend. The next page asks what the first remedy, changing the data, does.

steps.label: Changing the data
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that on the hard task 1000 against 100 already presses recall to 14.9%. This page asks what the first remedy, changing the data by copying the rare class or dropping the majority class, does. Oversampling: redraw 980 more points from the 20 rare points with replacement, making the training set 1000 plus 1000. Undersampling: keep only 20 of the 1000 majority points at random without replacement, making it 20 plus 20. The same SVM with C equal to 1, the data and test set of the first page, means of 20 runs. Results: plain, 1000 plus 20, recall 5.9%, precision 74.5%, accuracy 98.1%; oversampling, 1000 plus 1000, TP 68.15 and FP 605.55, recall 68.2%, precision 10.1%, accuracy 87.5%; undersampling, 20 plus 20, TP 77.05 and FP 756.7, recall 77.1%, precision 9.2%, accuracy 84.7%. Example: oversampling recall is 68.15 over 100, 68.2%, and precision is 68.15 over 68.15 plus 605.55, 10.1%. The price: the rare class is found again but precision falls to about 10% and accuracy to 85% to 88%. The next page asks whether dropping only the majority points far from the boundary is better, since over- and undersampling are random.

steps.label: Focused undersampling
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that over- and undersampling lift recall to 68% and 77% but give many false alarms. This page asks whether dropping only the majority points that are far from the boundary and carry no information is better. This is the source's focused undersampling; the concrete steps are this lecture's implementation: first train an SVM with C equal to 1 on the 20 plus 1000 points; second, compute decision values for the 1000 majority points and keep the m with the largest values, the ones most like the rare class; third, retrain with the 20 rare points plus these m; m is 20, 60, 100 or 200. In the figure the horizontal axis is m, with 1000 at the right, which is the plain SVM. Recall is 82.7%, 11.5%, 8.3%, 6.0%, 5.9%; accuracy 58.0%, 97.2%, 97.6%, 98.1%, 98.1%. Keeping 20 gives TP 82.7 and FP 2126.05, more false alarms than the 757 of random undersampling; keeping 20 and keeping 60 differ a lot. How far the target distribution should be shifted is an open problem, as the source says. The next page asks what happens when the data is left alone and the classifier's costs are changed.

steps.label: Changing the costs
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the number of majority points kept by focused undersampling is hard to set. This page asks what happens when the data is left alone and the classifier's costs are changed. This is the source's cost-sensitive remedy. SVM: the C for the rare class is 50 times that of the majority, weights 25.5 against 0.51. AdaBoost: 100 stumps, with the initial weight of the rare class multiplied by w equal to 1, 10 or 50 and then normalised; the weights of KP25 were designed for hard samples anyway. Means of 20 runs. Results: the plain SVM has recall 5.9% and precision 74.5%; with C 50 times for the rare class, TP 70.2 and FP 619.3, recall 70.2% and precision 10.2%; AdaBoost with w equal to 1 has recall 20.1% and precision 54.7%; w equal to 10, recall 48.3% and precision 23.1%; w equal to 50, recall 61.9% and precision 14.2%. Example: the SVM precision is 70.2 over 70.2 plus 619.3, which is 10.2%. As with changing the data, TP and FP rise together and precision falls. The next page asks what to remember.

steps.label: What to remember
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that, like changing the data, changing the costs raises TP and FP together and lowers precision. This page asks what should be remembered. How to remember, in the source's words: the harm of imbalance does not come from the numbers being different but from the interaction of the preference for simplicity with the rare class. Two remedies: change the data, that is resample, with oversampling, undersampling and focused undersampling, recall up and precision down; or change the costs, that is weight, with the SVM's class weights and AdaBoost's initial weights, recall up and precision down. The common myth is that high accuracy is enough. All-majority also has 98.0%; evaluation must look at how many are caught and how many false alarms, that is recall and precision, not accuracy alone. A reminder from the source: class imbalance matters a lot in practice and designers must be aware of it and of the remedies. This is the last page of the main line. The next page is an extension: put the treatments into one figure and see whether one clearly wins.

steps.label: Extension: comparing remedies
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said there are two remedies: change the data or change the costs. This extension page asks whether, with the four treatments in one figure and a metric that can see the rare class, one clearly wins. In the figure the horizontal axis is recall and the vertical axis precision; blue circles are the SVM and orange squares the decision tree with at least 5 points per leaf; each has four treatments: plain, oversampling, undersampling and cost-sensitive. Cost-sensitive means leaving the data alone and changing the classifier's costs. The higher the recall, the lower the precision. Balanced accuracy is the average of recall and specificity, where specificity is the share of majority points judged right, TN over 5000; all-majority is 0 plus 1 over 2, which is 0.50. Example: the plain SVM is 0.0585 plus 4998 over 5000, divided by 2, about 0.53. Balanced accuracy: SVM plain 0.53, oversampling 0.78, undersampling 0.81, cost-sensitive 0.79; decision tree 0.60, 0.66, 0.80, 0.69. No one clearly wins; the difference is the trade-off. The next page has two exercises.

steps.label: Extension: exercises
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that no one clearly wins and the difference is the trade-off. This page is the exercises. Exercise 1: 1000 negatives and 10 positives, the positives being the rare class. A judges everything negative; B catches 6 of the 10 positives and raises 40 false alarms among the negatives. What are the accuracy and the recall of A and of B? Exercise 2: what is the balanced accuracy of A and of B? The hint is that balanced accuracy is recall plus specificity over 2, with specificity equal to TN over 1000. Work them out first; the next page is the worked solution.

steps.label: Extension: worked solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page set two exercises. Exercise 1: A has TP 0, FN 10, FP 0 and TN 1000; its accuracy is 1000 over 1010, which is 0.990, and its recall is 0. B has TP 6, FN 4, FP 40 and TN 960; its accuracy is 966 over 1010, which is 0.956, and its recall is 6 over 10, which is 0.6. Exercise 2: A's balanced accuracy is 0 plus 1 over 2, which is 0.5; B's specificity is 960 over 1000, which is 0.96, and its balanced accuracy is 0.6 plus 0.96 over 2, which is 0.78. Check: A's accuracy is higher than B's yet it catches no rare point; B catches 60% but its precision is only 6 over 46, about 0.13, which is the trade-off. This is the last page of KP26; the next KP is the following unit of chapter 4.
